source.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Huai Hong; Yi-Ran Zhao; Wei Tang; Yang Deng; Yu Rong; Wenxuan Zhang

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper tests knowledge specialization and superposition in LLM MLPs using concept-specific masking and a specialization score, rather than reproducing the original toy-model method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own measurements of knowledge specialization, including concept-specific vector masking, model-scale comparisons, training checkpoints, concept-frequency comparisons, and fine-tuning experiments. Cited results from other work and the reported benchmark construction details are not separate findings about the claim.
record.test_reason: Each MLP value vector is one intermediate neuron's output weight. The study ablates the neurons most activated by a concept and measures how selectively concept knowledge is lost (PSS). Low PSS is explicitly read as knowledge superposition. It reports how this varies with model size and concept frequency in 20 real LLMs, which bears on V4 (knowledge spread across neurons) and on V2 (capacity and importance). Not a toy-model replication.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that more capable LLMs concentrate related knowledge in fewer, more specialized MLP value vectors, while weaker models spread it diffusely (more superposition). They also claim that controlled fine-tuning shows a causal link from specialization to better knowledge-task performance and less hallucination.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses concept-related question activations to select MLP value vectors, masks them, and measures concept-specific versus general accuracy through PSS; it does not use the original toy-model setup or its feature-geometry measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported specialization varies with model size, concept popularity/frequency, pretraining stage, and which parameter vectors are masked or fine-tuned.

fits_no_version.finding: In OLMo-2-7B, PSS stays near zero through step 510k and rises only after about step 610k, alongside accuracy gains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neuron-level knowledge specialization (reduced superposition) emerges late in pretraining at fixed model size.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning only the most-activated MLP value vectors (FT-PV) gives the best accuracy and lowest hallucination metrics. Its PSS gains lie within the reported uncertainty.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Targeted training of concept-selective neurons improves knowledge use.

record.problems: The study only examines MLP parameter vectors, uses Wikipedia page views as a proxy for pretraining frequency, and tests models no larger than 14B parameters. Several figure results have no exact values in the text. The Table 2 LLaMA2-7B PSS values are reproduced as printed, although their scale is unusual relative to the paper's other PSS reports.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible result rows were omitted. Table 2 MCQ, open-ended generation, semantic entropy, and local intrinsic dimension values were not recorded because they do not directly measure specialization or the representation distribution named in these claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy networks, sparsity transition or geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes the sharing; whether important features get dedicated single dimensions rather than merely more selective neuron sets.
SAE recovery of sparse features; attention modules; models above 14B.
All of it; no SAEs are used.

missing.what: Open-ended generation PSS vs performance across 20 models: Pearson 0.88, Spearman 0.84
Masking 5–10% of concept-related vectors improves accuracy on unrelated questions across models

record.verdict_notes: PSS is an ablation-selectivity score over top-k% neurons, averaged over k from 10% to 50%. It is an indirect proxy for superposition, not a geometric measure. The Table 2 LLaMA2-7B PSS (about 0.67) is inconsistent with Fig. 2 (about 0.05). The fine-tuning PSS differences are within the stated ± values, so the record's 'partial' states for r23/r25/r26/r28/r30/r31 are not supported. Figure 3 compares release generations, not capacity.

versions.untested_parts: No small toy networks, feature-to-dimension ratios, feature co-activation sparsity, or direction geometry are tested.

The paper tests specialization of knowledge across MLP value vectors, but does not directly establish a general limited-capacity account in which important features receive dedicated dimensions and other features share them.
It does not test alternative causes of polysemanticity or whether polysemantic neurons alone are evidence of superposition.
It measures knowledge distribution over MLP value vectors, not feature spread across neurons or SAE recovery.
The paper treats MLP value vectors as analysis units, but does not measure whether features are one-dimensional directions or assess their geometric orientation.

rows.operation_detail: Related concept-specific masking results into Parameter Specialization Score (PSS) and compared it with SpecWiki performance.
rows.measure: Correlation between PSS and SpecWiki performance
rows.note: The paper reports a strong positive association across the 20-model aggregate; it does not give individual plotted values in the text.
rows.check: This is a cross-model correlation with SpecWiki accuracy, not a capacity manipulation. Most of the 20 models are 6–8B, yet PSS ranges from about 0.01 to 0.16 (Fig. 2). Size-matched models therefore differ widely in sharing, so capacity alone does not explain it (partial for V2). Low PSS in every model does show diffuse knowledge (V4).

relationships.condition: Within-family size scaling (Qwen1.5 0.5B–14B, Gemma2 2B/9B) and concept frequency (LLaMA2-7B, Qwen2/2.5-7B)
relationships.reason: PSS rises from 0.019 to 0.184 with Qwen1.5 size and from 0.057 to 0.138 for Gemma2. Frequent concepts get more specialized neurons (r2–r8, r20–r21).
relationships.display_finding: The specialization score (PSS) rose from 0.019 to 0.184 across Qwen1.5 sizes and from 0.057 to 0.138 across Gemma2 sizes. Frequent concepts received more specialized neurons.

relationships.condition: Models of similar size (about 6–8B) from different families and releases
relationships.reason: PSS varies roughly tenfold among similar-sized models and tracks release date and accuracy. Neuron sharing therefore depends on training, not capacity alone (r1).

relation.reason: Concept-related MLP-vector masking measures selective versus general knowledge loss; the authors explicitly interpret low PSS as knowledge superposition.

tranche.reason: Tests knowledge sharing and specialization in pretrained real LLMs, a new setting relative to the original toy models.

source_check.notes: PSS is an ablation-based selectivity proxy, not a direct feature-to-dimension allocation measure; capacity causation remains untested. The authors' conclusion is paraphrased accurately, but hallucination reduction is assessed through semantic entropy and LID proxies.

statements.correction: §4.2/Figure 2: PSS varies across similarly sized models and is associated with SpecWiki accuracy and release date; Pearson R=0.92, p=1.41e-08; Spearman=0.93, p=4.87e-09. Capacity and training history are not independently manipulated.
statements.problem: The roughly tenfold difference is not stated numerically in the text; individual Figure 2 scores are not tabulated. Variation at similar parameter counts does not independently identify training history as its cause.
